facts.bodyText: Skip to the evidence am Ada Mensah Embedded firmware Explore the work ↗ Evidence ↗ MOSSLINK / A FICTIONAL PORTFOLIO STUDY 1 2 3 01 / THE QUESTION Between code and the bench. How do you connect a firmware decision to something you can actually observe? I wrote the firmware, scheduled the power states and built the bring-up fixture for Mosslink, an environmental sensor. Firmware is code that controls a physical device. ↓ Follow the connection 02 / THE CONNECTION Make the response observable. The fixture connects a board response to a bench observation. 01 Command 02 Board 03 Fixture 04 Observe Ada wrote the firmware and scheduled its power states. Firmware is code that controls a physical device. Bring-up means checking a new board's basic operation. A colleague designed the PCB and analogue front end. Follow the arrows: command → board → fixture → observation. Connections explain relationships, not electrical wiring. 03 / THE EVIDENCE A connection. Not a leap. I connect firmware decisions to bench observations through power-state scheduling and the bring-up fixture, while keeping the evidence limits visible. LONGEST RUN 72 hours Observed on the bench. BATTERY PROJECTION 2 years From bench current readings and an assumed reporting cycle. Read the scope of the evidence ↘ THE SCOPE MATTERS What the bench can tell us. Back to the question ↑ The longest run was 72 hours. Two years is a projection from bench current readings and an assumed reporting cycle. Forty engineering samples were assembled. Six were tested on the bench. None went to customers. One preliminary emissions check passed. Full qualification is unfinished. Ada wrote the firmware, scheduled the power states and built the bring-up fixture. A colleague designed the PCB and analogue front end. Ada and Mosslink are fictional. Illustrative bench model: shapes and connections are explanatory, not a photograph, circuit diagram, wiring plan or measured signal. Illustrative bench model / shapes and connections are explanatory
